analysis.one_liner: Limits tobacco advertising near schools and to youth audiences, but permanently strips the FDA of any authority over tobacco.
analysis.headline: The bill — modest tobacco ad limits paired with a blanket ban on FDA tobacco regulation — died in the Senate Commerce Committee with zero cosponsors and never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar cigarette and smokeless tobacco ads on billboards near schools, in youth-heavy magazines, at stadiums, on public transit, and paid product placement in movies and video games. It would also require states to pass youth-access laws (ID checks, vending machine rules, no free samples) as a condition of federal substance-abuse grants. But its final section goes the other way: it declares that no federal law gives the Food and Drug Administration any authority to regulate tobacco in any manner — closing off the toughest regulatory path, which the FDA had just begun to use. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and died there.
analysis.who_benefits: Tobacco manufacturers gain the most: in exchange for accepting advertising limits with many exceptions, they would be permanently exempted from FDA regulation. Magazine and billboard advertising companies keep most tobacco ad revenue, since the billboard ban applies only within 500 feet of schools and magazines are covered only if more than 15 percent of subscribers are under 18. State substance-abuse programs gain a new enforcement funding stream.

how_it_helps.text: Bars cigarette and smokeless tobacco ads on billboards within 500 feet of elementary or secondary schools, with an exception for street-level signs at stores that sell tobacco [S3]
Bans tobacco ads in publications where subscribers under 18 exceed 15 percent, in arenas and stadiums, and on buses, trains, and transit platforms [S3]

Prohibits paying to place cigarette brands as props in movies, in videos, on video game machines, or in family amusement centers, with a grandfather clause for brand names already shared with non-tobacco products as of 1995 [S3]

Conditions federal substance-abuse grants to states, starting in fiscal 1998, on state laws requiring photo ID for tobacco sales to anyone who appears under 26, restricting vending machines, banning free distribution and coupons in most settings, hiding product displays from customers, and banning sales of single 'loosies' [S2][S3]
Lets states use their federal grant money to enforce those youth-access laws [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers and advertisers lose some marketing channels and bear compliance costs, but the far larger benefit to them is the permanent FDA exemption. The public pays by losing the FDA as a potential regulator of tobacco — at the time the agency was asserting jurisdiction over tobacco marketing aimed at children — and by keeping tobacco advertising legal nearly everywhere else.

drawbacks.text: Section 5 would amend the federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act so that 'nothing in this Act or any other Act' gives the FDA any authority to regulate tobacco or tobacco products in any manner [S3] — a sweeping preclusion that would wipe out the FDA's 1996 rules on tobacco sales and marketing to minors, a far stronger set of protections than this bill's advertising limits

The advertising restrictions are narrow and full of exceptions: the billboard ban applies only within 500 feet of schools; stadium ads are allowed at concession stands and at any event the sponsor certifies is at least 75 percent adult; mail-order coupons and point-of-sale signs remain allowed; and shared brand names in use before 1995 are grandfathered [S3]

The youth-access provisions work only by conditioning federal substance-abuse grants on state legislation, so states that forgo the grants face no requirement at all, and the conditions do not begin until fiscal 1998 [S2][S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The advertising limits and grant conditions would have given youth-protection efforts a modest push, but the trade at the bill's core is a bad one for the public: narrow marketing rules with numerous carve-outs in exchange for a permanent statutory shield keeping the FDA — the agency with the strongest enforcement tools — out of tobacco entirely. An honest supporter of tobacco marketing limits would have to acknowledge that this bill forecloses more regulation than it creates.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or a vote, so the bill died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Wendell Ford of Kentucky, a Democrat, introduced the Tobacco Products Control Act of 1997 on January 23, 1997 [S1][S5]
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S5]
No further action appears in the record; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and it expired when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999 [S1][S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill's death left both sides roughly where they started: tobacco companies avoided the ad restrictions but also failed to lock in the statutory ban on FDA regulation, leaving the FDA's own 1996 youth-marketing rules in place to be fought out in court. Nobody secured the outcome they wanted from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; tobacco firms dodged ad limits but no FDA ban

for.name: Sen. Wendell Ford
for.role: U.S. Senator from Kentucky; bill's sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its accompanying remarks on the Senate floor; it was read twice and referred to the Commerce Committee

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it died in committee without any action

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no senator cosponsored the bill, so partisan lines never formed; the sole sponsor was a Democrat from tobacco-growing Kentucky.

industries.note: The bill would accept narrow advertising limits — near-school billboards, youth-heavy magazines, movie placement — while permanently barring the FDA from regulating tobacco in any manner, locking the industry out of the strongest form of federal oversight. Its interest runs against the public's, since the public's gain in the FDA provision's absence is the industry's loss.

Publishers and outdoor ad companies would lose some tobacco revenue from the school-zone billboard ban and the youth-readership rule, but the 15 percent threshold and point-of-sale exceptions preserve most placements. Their interest in keeping tobacco ad dollars runs against the public-health purpose of the restrictions.

In states that take the federal grants, retailers would face ID checks, vending machine limits, behind-the-counter displays, and a ban on selling single cigarettes, but the same grant framework funds enforcement and the bill shields tobacco from FDA rules that could have restricted sales far more broadly.
